title: Thermodynamic inference from noisy single-molecule time series
authors: Todd R. Gingrich, Oleg A. Igoshin, Anatoly B. Kolomeisky, Dmitrii E. Makarov
abstract: Single-molecule or single-particle tracking measurements inherently yield noisy microscopic trajectories, often significantly constrained by the diffraction limit and by the finite rate at which photons are emitted and counted. Here we study systematically the resulting effects of finite spatial and temporal resolution on one's ability to discern and quantify the arrow of time in microscopic trajectories. Given an experimental time series Y(t) degraded by noise, we consider the problem of estimating the entropy production associated with the corresponding microscopic variable X(t) using two strategies. The first attempts to infer the statistical properties of X(t) from those of Y(t) before estimating the entropy production. The second uses the experimental observable as a proxy for the true microscopic observable, with the entropy production estimator applied directly to Y(t). We prove that both strategies result in lower bounds on the true entropy production. Importantly, noise-degraded observables Y(t) undergo non-Markovian dynamics even when X(t) are Markovian, and non-Markovian entropy production estimators are advantageous. We further note nontrivial interplay between spatial and temporal resolution: in the presence of detection noise, improving the temporal resolution alone may lead to poorer rather than better entropy production estimates.
summary: This paper develops theoretical methods to estimate entropy production in molecular motors using noisy, time-resolved single-molecule tracking data. It rigorously compares multiple estimation strategies—including direct Markov estimators and bounds derived from fluctuation theorems—showing that noise fundamentally limits accuracy. The key takeaway is the necessity of advanced techniques, like non-Markovian inference or TUR analysis, to recover true thermodynamic quantities despite experimental limitations.
main_problem: The core problem is systematically quantifying how measurement noise (finite spatial/temporal resolution) degrades the ability to estimate fundamental thermodynamic quantities, specifically entropy production ($\dot{S}$), from noisy single-molecule trajectories.
main_result: Both standard inference strategies result in lower bounds on the true entropy production; furthermore, non-Markovian estimators are advantageous because noise can induce apparent non-Markovian dynamics even if the underlying process is Markovian.
method: The authors compare two main estimation strategies: (1) inferring the underlying kinetic matrix from noisy data, and (2) applying thermodynamic inference directly to the observed variable using high-order Markov estimators or fluctuation theorems (like TUR).
model_or_system: The analysis uses general stochastic processes modeled as continuous-time Markov chains ($X(t)$), applied specifically to molecular motors (e.g., F1FO ATPase) and diffusion processes, where the measurement yields a noisy observable $Y(t)$.
key_observables: Entropy production rate ($\dot{S}$), effective current ($\langle j_Y angle$), and variance ($\langle \delta j_Y^2 angle$).
important_parameters: Measurement time interval ($	au$), noise magnitude ($\epsilon$), and the underlying transition rates of the system.
main_assumptions: The methods often assume knowledge or invertibility of the measurement error matrix $R$, which is a major limitation; alternatively, they rely on rigorous bounds like the Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation (TUR).
figures_summary: Figures compare various estimators ($\langle\dot{S}angle_{Markov}$ vs. corrected/true values) across different noise levels and time resolutions for specific models (e.g., 8-state systems, random walks), showing performance degradation or recovery.
paper_structure: The paper develops the problem by first establishing general theoretical bounds (KL divergence, TUR) and then applying these concepts to concrete physical examples like molecular motors and diffusion processes, comparing multiple estimation techniques systematically.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous framework for analyzing experimental data from non-equilibrium systems where measurements are inherently noisy. The focus on the interplay between measurement resolution and thermodynamic inference is crucial for interpreting single-molecule biophysics experiments.
